findings.title: Negative offset is passed straight to queryset slicing, which Django rejects
findings.body: In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when enable_advanced_features is set and cursor.offset < 0, the code slices `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start_offset. Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing and raise ValueError ("Negative indexing is not supported"). The cursor offset comes from the client-controlled `cursor` query parameter (Cursor.from_string now accepts negative ints), so a crafted cursor produces an unhandled 500 for any admin who sends `optimized_pagination=true`. The branch does not deliver the advertised behaviour of reaching data beyond normal bounds.

findings.title: Prev-cursor path passes an unclamped, possibly negative offset to queryset slicing
findings.body: The new line `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` only clamps for next cursors. For a prev cursor, a negative offset (which Cursor now accepts from user input via from_string) becomes a negative slice start in `queryset[start_offset:stop]`, which Django raises ValueError on. This is reachable by any user of every BasePaginator-based endpoint, not just the audit log endpoint, and turns bad input into a 500. Also, for next cursors the silent clamp to 0 changes behaviour: a negative offset used to fail loudly and now is quietly treated as 0, so it can return the first page instead of an error.

findings.title: Comment claims permissions are enforced at queryset level, but the code does not do that
findings.body: The comment says negative offsets are 'safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level' and that the code 'enables access to data beyond normal pagination bounds'. The queryset is only filtered by organization_id and the optional actor/event filters in the endpoint; no per-row authorization is applied in the paginator. The enable_advanced_features flag is also derived from `is_superuser or has_global_access` in the endpoint, which is a coarse gate that the paginator itself never checks. This comment documents a security assumption that is false and will mislead future maintainers into relying on it.

findings.title: Experimental paginator is switched on by a user-supplied query parameter
findings.body: The new `optimized_pagination=true` query parameter selects a different paginator class and enables the advanced negative-offset path for superusers and global-access members. This is an unannounced public behaviour toggle on an endpoint whose publish_status is EXPERIMENTAL, with no feature flag, no documentation, and no tests. Any change in cursor semantics would then be exposed to clients that set this parameter, and the two code paths would need to be maintained in parallel.

findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates BasePaginator.get_result with only a minor change
findings.body: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result is almost a line-for-line copy of BasePaginator.get_result, and the same is true of get_item_key and value_from_cursor. The only real difference is the negative-offset branch, which is the broken path described above. The two copies will drift, and fixes to one (for example the typo-related ordering logic in build_queryset) will not reach the other. The paginator should either be a thin subclass with an overridden offset rule or be removed.

findings.title: No tests for the new pagination behaviour or the new paginator
findings.body: The PR adds OptimizedCursorPaginator, changes offset clamping in BasePaginator.get_result, and adds a request-driven code path in the audit log endpoint, but includes no tests. There is no coverage for negative cursor offsets, prev cursors with negative offsets, the optimized_pagination toggle, or the permission gating. The existing audit log endpoint tests do not exercise the new branch.

findings.title: Comment in Cursor.__init__ describes a feature that is not implemented here
findings.body: The added comment says negative offsets 'enable efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets', but Cursor simply stores int(offset). The actual efficiency claim is not true: negative offsets either raise in Django slicing or are clamped to 0 elsewhere. Also, removing the implicit non-negative guarantee on Cursor.offset affects every consumer of cursors, and that is not mentioned anywhere.

findings.title: PR description is a placeholder and does not explain the change
findings.body: The PR description reads only 'Test 1'. It gives no motivation for the new paginator, no explanation of why negative offsets are needed, no description of the optimized_pagination toggle, and no rollout or risk notes. A reviewer cannot evaluate the intent or the risk of changing shared cursor behaviour from this text.
